A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VLA-Cache research. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original LIBERO and SIMPLER evaluations, token-selection and token-budget ablations, and Kinova Jaco2 experiments, including success rates and computational measurements.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds OpenVLA-OFT evaluations, control-frequency measurements, dynamic-background tests, and further ablations.

M1.justification: Both versions use patch similarity to select static tokens, attention to exclude task-relevant tokens, entropy-based layer adaptation, and selective KV-cache reuse. Splitting the algorithm and testing additional architectures do not establish a changed proposed procedure; the object-mask alternative is an ablation.

E1.justification: LIBERO, both SIMPLER settings, and the four real-world tasks remain. V2 adds PickPot evaluations with moving background objects and people, plus fixed-camera and moving wrist-camera inputs through OpenVLA-OFT. These extend input conditions within the retained manipulation tasks.

E2.justification: FastV and SparseVLM remain the OpenVLA acceleration comparators. V2 adds unaccelerated OpenVLA-OFT comparisons, an object-mask relevance variant using Efficient Track Anything in Table 8, and an explicit OpenVLA baseline row in the component ablation. Newly cited ToMe, PuMer, and MADTP are not evaluated.

E3.justification: V2 adds policy control frequency as an evaluation metric across the principal comparisons and evaluates the action-chunking OpenVLA-OFT configuration. New controlled experiments vary background motion, relevance proxies, token budgets, and relevance thresholds. The original default thresholds, fine-tuning budget, and hardware remain; newly disclosed real-world trial procedures do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component and token-budget ablations, v2 tests robustness to moving backgrounds, compares attention against object-mask relevance selection, and studies OpenVLA-OFT sensitivity to token budgets and relevance thresholds (Tables 7–10). These substantially expand evidence about robustness and the selection mechanism.

E5.justification: Appendix E.4 newly specifies 20 randomized trials for PickPot and PutSausage and 30 for PlaceCube and WipeTable, with success/failure counts. This discloses evaluation repetitions rather than establishing an increase in runs. Neither version reports confidence intervals, seed-level variability, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Most original LIBERO and SIMPLER scores are retained. V2 adds control-frequency results and substantial OpenVLA-OFT, robustness, and sensitivity results; its Table 2 reports 96.8% versus 97.4% success and 65.10 versus 78.98 Hz for OpenVLA-OFT without versus with caching. Real-world WipeTable success changes from 73.0% to 73.3%, and the average from 84.5% to 84.6%. Component-ablation FLOP entries are omitted.

T1.justification: The entropy-based reuse definition, KV-update equations, FLOP savings model, and selection-overhead analysis are mathematically retained. V1's complexity appendix becomes Appendix C in v2. Renotation and condensation of repeated inference equations introduce no substantive assumptions, proofs, or derivations.

C1.justification: The central claim remains training-free acceleration through adaptive temporal token reuse with little loss of task success. V2 adds an explicit abstract claim of a 15% control-frequency increase and emphasizes compatibility with optimized, high-frequency VLA architectures. These extend the claimed benefits without replacing the core contribution.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive applicability qualifications: extensive motion reduces reuse, other decoder backbones remain untested, and standalone diffusion policies are outside the method's direct scope. It also interprets the object-mask comparison through contextual relevance and discusses robustness under camera motion. The main interpretations of the retained benchmarks remain stable.

D1.justification: V2 adds a project-page pointer for code and videos and clarifies real-world success criteria, randomization, fixed-horizon single-attempt evaluation, and absence of intervention. Most hardware, preprocessing, precision, sampling, and fine-tuning details already appear in v1 and are relocated or condensed.

R1.justification: V2 adds discussion and citations for ToMe, PuMer, MADTP, π0-FAST, HiRT, OpenVLA-OFT, Gemma2, and Efficient Track Anything, while dropping several preliminary-background references. It more explicitly positions caching as complementary to high-frequency architectures. The original distinction from pruning and retraining-based acceleration remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, acceleration discussion, and experimental narrative undergo extensive rewriting. Preliminary material is incorporated into Methodology, implementation receives a separate section, the algorithm is split, and the appendices are reorganized into limitations, impact, complexity, inference, and experimental sections.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. Figures 1 and 2 are redrawn, simulation and real-world task illustrations are merged, and the main visualization gains dynamic-background and wrist-camera panels. Tables gain frequency columns and model rows, new analysis tables appear, and retained appendix visualizations are relocated and renumbered.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central practical-efficiency argument through control-frequency measurements, an already optimized OpenVLA-OFT baseline, and targeted robustness and relevance-selection tests. These address important gaps in v1's evidence, while clearer limitations and trial protocols improve interpretability. Local reporting errors temper the gain: Table 7 implies approximately 29% FLOP and 26% latency reductions, not the stated 42% and 35%; Table 11's pooled counts imply 81% and 84%, whereas its displayed percentages are task averages. These problems do not outweigh the substantial evidential improvements.
